Caliber Mining is based in Chandrapur, Maharashtra and does coal digging and transport work for big mining companies. Almost all its money comes from just 2 companies under Coal India. 

Northern Coalfields gives it 44% of total business. Western Coalfields gives most of remaining. If either of these 2 clients cuts back orders, Caliber revenue drops fast. 

Right now, order book is ₹9,551 crore and FY26 revenue was ₹1,678 crore with ₹158 crore profit. 

Coal India sells some of its coal through online auctions where buyers bid above fixed prices. In August 2026, buyers paid 59% more than fixed price on average. This is much higher than 35% premium last year. 

When Coal India earns more money per tonne of coal, it can spend more on hiring companies like Caliber Mining to dig and transport that coal. Caliber gets 85% of its work from Coal India units. 

Coal India coal stocks at power plants have fallen to just 8 days worth, keeping demand tight

Caliber Mining owns and leases 1,911 vehicles including mining trucks, excavators, and trailers. Running this fleet costs money. Fuel and power alone eat up 47% of what company spends on operations. 

In FY26, Caliber made ₹1,678 crore revenue and kept 25.7% as EBITDA, which is much better than competitors like Power Mech at 11.6%. Before its IPO, company had borrowed heavily with debt 1.63 times its equity. ₹208 crore from IPO went toward repaying loans. 

Revenue grew from ₹953 crore in FY24 to ₹1,678 crore in FY26

The club of Indian listed firms selling over ₹1 lakh crore a year has doubled in five years, from 13 to 26.

HOW TO READ IT
Each card is one listed company whose yearly sales crossed the ₹1 lakh crore mark. Banks, lenders and insurers are not counted. A card shows the company's name and its sales in lakh crore for the year to March 2026.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- Reliance tops the list at ₹10.8 lakh crore in sales for the year to March 2026, more than double its ₹4.9 lakh crore five years earlier.
- 12 new names have joined the club since the year to March 2021, while all 13 original members are still on the list.
- The year to March 2026 count is 26, drawn from 4,613 listed companies, against 13 from 3,267 five years earlier.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
Sales here are a company's revenue from operations for the year: the money it earned from selling its goods and services, from its own yearly accounts. For a company that owns others, it is the whole group's figure (consolidated), which includes every company it owns more than half of; a company without group accounts is counted on its own. The club is every listed company with sales of ₹1 lakh crore or more in the year to March 2026 (26 companies), and the same for the year to March 2021 (13). Banks, lenders and insurers are left out, because what they earn is interest and insurance money, not sales. In all, 4,613 listed companies (outside banks, lenders and insurers) filed yearly sales for 2026, and 3,267 for 2021. As a check against reading errors, a figure counts only when it agrees with the company's sales the year before (between half and double), its four quarters add up to it within 10%, and it fits the company's size (no more than ten times what it owns). A figure that fails a check still counts when the company states it in its own words in a document we hold for that year (Rajesh Exports and Coal India for 2026; Hindalco for 2021). Rajesh Exports' figure for 2021 could not be confirmed (it fails the checks and we hold no document for that year), so it is not counted for 2021, shown there as "not confirmed", and not marked new. 8 other companies whose 2021 figures in our data show ₹1 lakh crore or more are left out, because those figures fail the checks; each of them reports sales of under ₹10,000 crore for 2026. Vedanta is under the line: its own accounts give ₹78,437 crore for 2026, because they leave out the businesses it plans to split off into separate companies. Tata Motors split in two in 2025: the company that sells cars and Jaguar Land Rover kept the listing (shown for 2026 as Tata Motors (cars)), and its truck business is now listed separately. The members' sales are not added up: some members own others, so a total would count the same sales twice. Sales are not profit, and they grow with prices as well as with the amount sold. This says nothing about whether any company is good, cheap or well run.

Indian Steel Sector – Key Investor Takeaways

The domestic steel cycle appears to be entering a more favourable phase, supported by low inventories, improving demand and rising steel prices. The key question is whether this recovery can sustain long enough to drive FY27 earnings upgrades.

1. Domestic steel demand outlook

October–March is expected to be a strong period as construction and infrastructure activity accelerate after the monsoon.

Domestic HRC prices are now slightly above import parity, while inventories remain low. This creates potential for restocking-led demand during the busy season.

Rebar prices have also recovered sharply on tight supply, planned maintenance shutdowns and low inventories.

2. Steel prices have recovered significantly

In September, domestic prices reached approximately:
HRC: ₹61,700/tonne
Primary rebar: ₹57,300/tonne
Rebar had recovered from ~₹48,000/tonne in July.
August price movement:
Rebar: +10% MoM, +12% YoY
HRC: +2% MoM, +19% YoY
Stainless steel: +3% MoM, +17% YoY

The HRC recovery has been supported by tighter domestic supply and improving West Asia demand, while rebar benefited from maintenance shutdowns and inventory tightening.

3. Raw-material picture is mixed
Iron ore: Relatively soft. NMDC reduced prices earlier in response to weaker global iron-ore prices, although it subsequently increased lump-ore prices by ~₹150/tonne in September while leaving fines unchanged.
Coking coal: Prices remain elevated and are a key cost pressure. However, Chinese mine restarts could increase supply and potentially moderate coal prices.
Tata Steel and JSW Steel have an advantage from their relatively lower exposure to externally sourced coking coal.

SAIL has comparatively higher exposure to coke prices, making raw-material costs an important monitorable.

4. Global steel backdrop

US HRC prices have risen >30% from August levels, indicating strong pricing momentum.

China export HRC prices have remained relatively stable.

European steel prices are expected to improve through Q2/Q3, although European coking-coal costs are also expected to rise.

Global demand is increasingly being influenced by security of supply and potential supply-chain disruptions, rather than simply absolute price levels.

5. Company positioning

Tata Steel

Has significant flat-steel capacity and relatively lower external coking-coal exposure.

European operations could provide an additional earnings tailwind if European steel prices improve.

Q1 consolidated revenue was ₹60,794 crore (+14% YoY, -4% QoQ).

EBITDA was ₹9,264 crore (+25% YoY, -6% QoQ), broadly in line with estimates.

PAT was ₹2,664 crore (+21% YoY, -18% QoQ).
Sequential EBITDA decline was primarily due to lower volumes from planned maintenance shutdowns.

SAIL

Has higher operating leverage to recovering domestic rebar prices but also greater exposure to coke costs.

Adjusted Q1 revenue was ₹26,555 crore (+3% YoY, -14% QoQ).

Adjusted EBITDA was ₹4,462 crore (+72% YoY, -1% QoQ), comfortably ahead of consensus.

PAT was ₹1,644 crore (+121% YoY, -10% QoQ), also ahead of expectations.

JSW Steel / Jindal Steel
Both offer relatively strong volume-growth + steel-price leverage, making them sensitive to continued improvement in domestic realisations.

6. Coal India – key raw-material read-through

Coal India reported consolidated revenue of ₹46,255 crore (+8% YoY, -1% QoQ).

EBITDA adjusted for stripping activity was ₹10,238 crore (-9% YoY, -17% QoQ), broadly in line with estimates.

Reported EBITDA was ₹12,069 crore (-4% YoY, -5% QoQ), below consensus.
PAT was ₹8,852 crore (+1% YoY, -18% QoQ), ahead of estimates largely because of higher other income.

7. What to watch from here

Domestic steel realisations: The most important variable. Sustained HRC/rebar prices could trigger FY27 earnings upgrades.

Inventory: Low inventories provide a potential restocking catalyst during the October–March period.

Coking coal: A major swing factor for margins. Chinese mine restarts could provide some cost relief.

Infrastructure/auto demand: Continued government capex and construction activity should support volumes, while auto contract-price revisions provide some protection against price weakness.

Global steel prices: Particularly Europe and the US, which could influence export opportunities and consolidated earnings.

The sector is moving from a period of depressed realisations toward a potentially healthier pricing cycle, with low inventories + improving demand + supply discipline creating operating leverage; the sustainability of steel prices and coking-coal costs will determine whether this translates into FY27 earnings upgrades and further sector re-rating.
